title.narrative: NIHR DA 1: A task for community health workers? Mental health care for people in disadvantaged communities

description.narrative:
A low- and-middle-income country (LMIC) award led by the University of Witwatersrand, South Africa, which aims to develop a research proposal for the co-design, implementation, and evaluation of a community health worker-based service for screening for serious mental illness and supporting people living with serious mental illness (PLSMI) in a peri-urban community in Gauteng province, South Africa, that is integrated with primary health care services.
The government-implemented community health worker (CHW) programme expects CHWs to identify and refer cases of common mental disorders, gender-based violence, and drug, alcohol and child abuse. However, little training is provided on the skills necessary to fulfil these roles nor on the skills needed to support PLSMI.
Due to commence in January 2025, the twelve-month award intends to develop a research proposal for future research on a community health worker-based model for PLSMI through community engagement and involvement. Award activity initially focuses on understanding community health workers’ (CHWs) perceptions of serious mental illness and how they perceive their role in relation to PLSMI. It will involve engagement with community representatives and key stakeholders including decision-makers in order to better understand the experiences of PLSMI, and the existing and prospective role of CHWs and service providers in supporting CHWs to provide care for PLSMI. The focus on community engagement within this award will work to establish a core group of community representatives to ensure the integration of community representation, provide capacity-strengthening activities for community members and facilitate the co-development of a research proposal.

The project has four objectives:
1. To understand community health workers’ perceptions of serious mental illness, the role of traditional and biomedical treatments, and how they currently perceive their role concerning people living with serious mental illness. 2. To explore with community members the potential role of community health workers can play in supporting people living with serious mental illnesses. 3. To engage with healthcare providers and decision-makers on whether and how the publicly funded primary care system might integrate and support community health workers working with people living with serious mental illness. 4. To map the evidence for components of a community health worker-based service for people living with serious mental illness via an evidence map.
